slides: The chain.
This is my own method. It's how I make sure my development never skips a step, and never gets lost.
A chain is the vertical key sentence from the last lesson, written as quick notes on your scrap paper. Cause, and effect. From what the task asks about, to your result.
So before you write the paragraph, you draft the chain. Then you paste it into the paragraph, with a template.
Why? Well, nothing gets skipped, because every arrow turns into a sentence.
You don't get lost in the middle of the paragraph. You always know what the next sentence is.
And you see right away if your argument really gets to its result... or if there's a hole in it.
How long is a chain? About ten words per argument.
Like this one. Free buses. Cheaper than driving. Some drivers switch. Fewer cars. Less traffic.
Now, ten words is a guide. It's not a limit.
Don't drop a link you need just to keep it short. And don't fill it with links that say nothing new.
Short enough to write in thirty seconds. Complete enough that nothing's missing.
Now, the four checks. They're the difference between a chain, and a good chain.
Check one. Test every arrow. For every arrow, ask: why would this step lead to the next one?
If the answer is obvious and makes sense, keep it, and explain it in the paragraph.
If it's true only sometimes, add a condition.
And if it doesn't really follow... there's a missing step. Add it. Or, if you can't, then this argument isn't strong enough. Pick another one.
Let's test the camera chain.
Cameras installed, so offenders know they're recorded. Always? Only if they know the cameras exist. So I add a condition: the public is informed.
They know, so they're deterred. Why? Only if being recorded means a real chance of getting caught. So I explain: identification in real time.
Deterred, so less crime. In these areas, yes. But some of them may just move somewhere else. So I keep my claim precise: less crime in these areas.
Every weak arrow got an explanation, or a condition. And now the chain is solid.
Check two. No arrows that just rename the same thing.
Look at this. Students concentrate, so students pay attention. That's not a step. It's the same thing, in different words.
An arrow like that looks like development, but it adds nothing. In the paragraph, it turns into repetition.
And it's actually worse. It hides the real gap. How exactly does paying attention lead to better grades?
So, a quick test. Does the second box say something new? Something that could have failed to happen? If not, merge the two boxes.
Check three. The paragraph can't sound pasted.
If you just copy the arrows one after the other, it sounds like this. This will, this will, this will. It's a list, not a paragraph.
Instead: once cameras are installed. This, in turn. As a result. Mix up the connectors. Mix up how the sentences are built.
And put the explanation of each arrow inside the sentence, with 'because' or 'since'.
Here's a set of linking phrases for the arrows. Mix them.
For the first step: once, when, if.
For the next steps: this, in turn. As a result. Consequently. This means that.
Inside a sentence: which in turn. So that. Leading to.
To explain an arrow: because, since, as. And for a condition: as long as, provided that.
Now, one warning. A connector shows there's a link. It doesn't create one. Writing 'therefore' doesn't make a step follow. The arrow has to make sense first.
Check four. Use the chain for the other side too.
Write the opponent's chain, the same way. Cameras everywhere. Every movement recorded. People feel watched. Some avoid lawful gatherings. Public life suffers.
Then find its weakest arrow. That's your weakening. That's the heart of the rebuttal paragraph.
We'll do this properly in the lessons on weakening and the rebuttal paragraph. For now, just remember: chains work on both sides.
Let's fix a weak chain. The task: should phones be banned during lessons?
Here's a first draft. Ban phones. Students concentrate. Students pay attention. Better grades.

Concentrate, pay attention: that's a renaming arrow. Ban, so they concentrate... why? The mechanism is missing. And attention straight to better grades? That's a jump. And it's said as if it's certain.

So here's the fix. Phones banned in lessons. So no notifications, and less temptation. So longer stretches of attention, with no interruptions. So more of the material is understood the first time. So learning is likely to improve.
The mechanism is in. The renaming is gone. The jump is filled. And the result is hedged: likely to improve.
So. Draft the chain, from what the task asks about to the final result. About ten words.
Test every arrow. No renaming arrows. Write it so it doesn't sound pasted. And chain the other side too.
